claim: Two adult female rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta, both 7 kg) were used for electrophysiological recordings in this study.
source: Two adult female rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta, both 7 kg) were used for electrophysiological recordings in this study.
evidence: Direct statement about the experimental subjects used in the study.

claim: Increasing the size of a low-contrast stimulus improved behavioral performance in monkeys.
source: Consistent with previous findings in humans (Tadin et al., 2003), we found that increasing the size of a low-contrast stimulus improved behavioral performance (Figure 1D, dashed lines)
evidence: Experimental data from behavioral testing shown in Figure 1D, with citation to previous human studies.

claim: Under high-contrast conditions, behavioral performance worsened at larger stimulus sizes in monkeys.
source: while under high-contrast conditions, behavioral performance worsened at larger sizes (Figure 1D, solid lines).
evidence: Experimental data from behavioral testing shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Psychophysical performance was best for stimuli of medium intensity, with performance declining as contrast and size were increased.
source: Thus, paradoxically, psychophysical performance was best for stimuli of medium intensity, with performance declining as contrast and size were increased (Figure 1D, Wilcoxon rank sum test, p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: At 100% contrast, the psychophysical suppression index (SIpsy) was 0.42 ± 0.25 for monkey C.
source: At 100% contrast, the SIpsy of the psychometric function (mean ± s.d.) was 0.42 ± 0.25 for monkey C
evidence: Quantitative measurement from behavioral experiments.

claim: At 100% contrast, the psychophysical suppression index (SIpsy) was 0.54 ± 0.19 for monkey Y.
source: At 100% contrast, the SIpsy of the psychometric function (mean ± s.d.) was 0.42 ± 0.25 for monkey C and 0.54 ± 0.19 for monkey Y
evidence: Quantitative measurement from behavioral experiments.

claim: Monkeys were approximately half as likely to accurately perceive the motion of a large stimulus compared to a small one.
source: indicating that monkeys were approximately half as likely to accurately perceive the motion of a large stimulus, compared to a small one.
evidence: Interpretation of the SIpsy values measured in the experiments.

claim: 165 single units were analyzed from area MT.
source: We analyzed data from 165 single units, with 2–8 cells being available on any given day.
evidence: Direct statement about the number of neurons recorded.

claim: 2-8 cells were available on any given recording day.
source: We analyzed data from 165 single units, with 2–8 cells being available on any given day.
evidence: Direct statement about the recording methodology.

claim: The mean neuronal suppression index (SIneu) for the MT population was 0.27.
source: For the MT population, the mean neuronal d' (SIneu = 0.27) was much less suppressed than the mean psychometric d' (SIpsy = 0.48, Figure 2D).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from neurophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The mean psychometric suppression index (SIpsy) was 0.48.
source: For the MT population, the mean neuronal d' (SIneu = 0.27) was much less suppressed than the mean psychometric d' (SIpsy = 0.48, Figure 2D).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The magnitude of neuronal surround suppression is too small to account for psychophysical suppression.
source: Our neurophysiological recordings revealed that the magnitude of the neuronal surround suppression of individual neurons is too small to account for psychophysical suppression.
evidence: Comparison of neuronal and behavioral suppression indices.

claim: Many MT neurons exhibited no surround suppression at all, even for stimuli extending beyond their receptive fields.
source: Moreover, many neurons exhibited no surround suppression at all, even for stimuli extending beyond their receptive fields (Born and Tootell, 1992)
evidence: Observation from neurophysiological recordings with citation to previous work.

claim: The selectivity of neurons without surround suppression to large stimuli routinely exceeded that of the monkeys.
source: and the selectivity of these neurons to large stimuli routinely exceeded that of the monkeys (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: Comparison of neuronal and behavioral selectivity shown in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: There was no evidence that neurons with strong surround suppression were more correlated with the animals' behavioral choices.
source: However, using choice probability analysis (Britten et al., 1996; Nienborg et al., 2012; Haefner et al., 2013), we found no evidence that neurons with strong surround suppression were more correlated with the animals' behavior choices
evidence: Analysis of choice probability data with citations to methodological references.

claim: The correlation between neuronal suppression index (SIneu) and choice probability was modestly negative (r = -0.14, P = 0.04).
source: indeed the correlation between SIneu and choice probability was modestly negative (Figure 2E; r = -0.14, P = 0.04).
evidence: Statistical analysis of the relationship between SIneu and choice probability shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The mean level of noise correlations was 0.099 ± 0.007.
source: The mean levels of noise correlations were typically on the order of 0.1 (0.099 ± 0.007), compatible with previous reports (Zohary et al., 1994; Bair et al., 2001; Huang and Lisberger, 2009).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from multi-electrode recordings with citations to previous studies.

claim: The strength of noise correlations was independent of motion direction.
source: Their strength was independent of motion direction or stimulus size (Wilcoxon rank sum test for direction, 94% of experiments with p>0.05
evidence: Statistical analysis of noise correlations across different stimulus conditions.

claim: The strength of noise correlations was independent of stimulus size (P = 0.55).
source: Their strength was independent of motion direction or stimulus size (Wilcoxon rank sum test for direction, 94% of experiments with p>0.05; for smaller and larger sizes, P = 0.55 Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Statistical analysis of noise correlations across different stimulus sizes shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Noise correlations and signal correlations are significantly correlated (r = 0.32, p<0.001) across the MT population.
source: The relationship illustrated by this example pair is characteristic of the population (Figure 4A), across which noise correlations and signal correlation are significantly correlated (r = 0.32, p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical analysis of the relationship between noise and signal correlations shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The magnitudes of noise correlations (rnoise) were not significantly different across types of neuron pairs (SS-SS, NS-NS, SS-NS).
source: Across the population, the magnitudes of rnoise were not significantly different across types of neuron pairs (Wilcoxon rank sum tests, p>0.86).
evidence: Statistical comparison of noise correlation magnitudes across neuron pair types.

claim: The correlation structure differed substantially for different cell classes (SS-SS, NS-NS, SS-NS).
source: However, the correlation structure differed substantially for different cell classes: For the NS-NS pairs, rnoise and rsignal tended to be correlated (Figure 4A, red dots).
evidence: Analysis of correlation structure across different neuron pair types shown in Figure 4A.

claim: For NS-NS pairs, noise correlation (rnoise) and signal correlation (rsignal) tended to be correlated.
source: For the NS-NS pairs, rnoise and rsignal tended to be correlated (Figure 4A, red dots).
evidence: Analysis of NS-NS neuron pairs shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Pairs of SS neurons showed less dependency of noise correlation on signal correlation compared to NS-NS pairs.
source: By contrast pairs of SS neurons showed less of a dependency of noise correlation on signal correlation (Figure 4A, blue dots).
evidence: Analysis of SS-SS neuron pairs shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The difference in the slopes of the lines relating signal and noise correlations was significantly lower for SS pairs than for NS pairs (ANCOVA, P = 0.03).
source: The difference in the slopes of the lines relating signal and noise correlations was significantly lower for the SS pairs than for the NS pairs (ANCOVA, P = 0.03, multiple comparison test) (Figure 4A, red and blue lines).
evidence: Statistical comparison of slopes between SS and NS neuron pairs shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Sampling from rate-matched sub-distributions of SS-SS and NS-NS pairs yielded significantly higher rnoise vs. rsignal slopes for the NS-NS sub-distributions (p<0.001).
source: Also, sampling from rate-matched sub-distributions of SS-SS and NS-NS pairs (Materials and methods) yielded significantly higher rnoise vs. rsignal slopes for the NS-NS sub-distributions (Figure 4B; Wilcoxon rank sum test, p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical analysis of rate-matched neuron pairs shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The reduction of noise correlation dependency on signal correlation did not depend on the categorical classification of SS and NS neurons.
source: Finally, the reduction of this rnoise dependency did not depend on the categorical classification of SS and NS neurons, as we obtained similar results using continuous values of the joint SIneu for pairs of neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C; linear correlation: (r = -0.232, p<0.0001).
evidence: Analysis using continuous values of suppression index shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There is a positive relationship between noise correlations and differential correlations (f'f') across neuronal pairs.
source: We calculated differential correlations for all neuronal pairs, and found that there is indeed a positive relationship between noise correlations and f'f' (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Analysis of differential correlations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The magnitude of information-limiting correlations is greater between NS-NS pairs than between SS-SS pairs (rNS-NS = 0.48, rSS-SS = 0.23, P = 0.08).
source: Furthermore, we find the same difference between SS-SS and NS-NS pairs as reported above (Figure 4A): the magnitude of the information-limiting correlations is greater between NS-NS pairs than between SS-SS pairs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E, rNS-NS = 0.48, rSS-SS = 0.23, P = 0.08).
evidence: Statistical comparison of information-limiting correlations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: While NS neurons are individually more informative for large stimuli than SS neurons, as a population they are more limited by their correlation structure than SS neurons.
source: In brief, while NS neurons are individually more informative for large stimuli than SS neurons, as a population they are more limited by their correlation structure than SS neurons.
evidence: Summary inference from the correlation structure analysis.

claim: The model suppression index was 0.48, matching the empirical behavioral suppression.
source: The suppression shown by the model is of the same magnitude as the empirical behaviour (Figure 5E, black), with the model SI being 0.48 (Figure 5C,E cyan).
evidence: Comparison of model predictions to behavioral data shown in Figure 5C and 5E.

claim: Both noise correlation structure and surround suppression were necessary to account for the decreased performance as a function of size.
source: We found that both the noise correlation structure and surround suppression were necessary to account for the decreased performance as a function of size, since models (Zohary et al., 1994) and (Shadlen et al., 1996) did not show any psychophysical suppression at all (SI = 0; data not shown).
evidence: Results from model simulations testing different components.

claim: A model with correlations and surround suppression but without their observed relationship exhibited only modest psychophysical suppression (SI = 0.28).
source: However, these components together were not sufficient to account for the observed behavioral results, since model (Abbott and Dayan, 1999) exhibited only modest psychophysical suppression (SI = 0.28; Figure 5C,E magenta).
evidence: Results from model simulation shown in Figure 5C and 5E.

claim: The relationship between surround suppression and correlation structure appears to have important consequences for motion perception.
source: Thus the relationship between surround suppression and correlation structure appears to have important consequences for motion perception.
evidence: Inference from comparison of different model variants.

claim: The surround-suppression-dependent correlation structure increases performance for small stimuli.
source: Perhaps more surprising is an increase in performance seen for small stimuli (Figure 5C,E).
evidence: Observation from model simulations shown in Figure 5C and 5E.

claim: The combined effect of correlation structure and surround suppression is an increase in the capacity of the MT population to discriminate the direction of very small stimuli, at the expense of large stimuli.
source: This suggests that the combined effect of correlation structure and surround suppression is an increase in the capacity of the MT population to discriminate the direction of very small stimuli, at the expense of large stimuli (see Discussion).
evidence: Inference from model simulation results.

claim: The suppression index decreased to 0.26 when the integration radius was increased to 15°.
source: Unsurprisingly the SI decreased with increasing integration radius, dropping to 0.26 when the radius was 15°, which is significantly less than that exhibited psychophysically by the monkeys (Figure 5E green, Wilcoxon rank sum test, p<0.001).
evidence: Results from model simulations with varying integration radius shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The overall model performance was unaffected by the integration radius parameter (ANOVA, P = 0.25).
source: The overall model performance, obtained by summing the performance across all sizes, was, however, unaffected by this parameter (ANOVA, P = 0.25).
evidence: Statistical analysis of model performance across different integration radii.

claim: A larger integration radius increases the performance at large sizes while decreasing the performance at small sizes.
source: This is due to the fact that a larger integration radius increases the performance at large sizes, while decreasing the performance at small sizes (Figure 5C).
evidence: Analysis of model behavior with different integration radii shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Behavioral suppression index could vary substantially according to the internal strategies used by the observer.
source: This suggests that behavioral SI could vary substantially according to the internal strategies used by the observer.
evidence: Inference from the effect of integration radius on model performance.

claim: Area MT was identified based on anatomical MRI scan, depth, prevalence of direction-selective neurons, receptive field size to eccentricity relationship, and white matter to grey matter transition from a dorsal-posterior approach.
source: Area MT was identified based on an anatomical MRI scan, as well as depth, prevalence of direction-selective neurons, receptive field size to eccentricity relationship, and white matter to grey matter transition from a dorsal-posterior approach.
evidence: Description of the methodology for identifying recording location.

claim: Linear microelectrode arrays (V-Probe, Plexon) with 16 contacts were used to record single-units.
source: We recorded single-units using linear microelectrode arrays (V-Probe, Plexon) with 16 contacts.
evidence: Description of recording equipment used.

claim: A brief stimulus duration (50 ms) was used to increase the difficulty of the task.
source: As in most human studies, we used a very brief stimulus duration (50 ms) (Tadin et al., 2003) in order to increase the difficulty of the task.
evidence: Explanation of experimental design choice with citation.

claim: Monkeys performed 20-40 repetitions of each distinct stimulus in a typical session.
source: In a typical session, the monkeys performed 20–40 repetitions of each distinct stimulus.
evidence: Description of experimental protocol.

claim: The firing rate during the 100-200 ms interval after stimulus onset was used to calculate neuronal d'.
source: To quantify the neuronal selectivity of both the single neurons and the population, we used the firing rate during the 100200 ms interval after stimulus onset to calculate the d'.
evidence: Description of data analysis methodology.

claim: The 100-200 ms time window was chosen because firing rates in response to preferred and null directions were significantly different (p<0.05) during this interval.
source: This interval was chosen because the firing rates in response to the preferred and null directions were significantly different (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E; p<0.05, t-test)
evidence: Justification for analysis time window based on statistical testing shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Spikes during the 100-200 ms time window were significantly correlated with the animals' behavioral choices.
source: and spikes during this time window were significantly correlated with the animals' behavioral choices (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C)
evidence: Analysis of spike-choice correlation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Other time windows between 60-300 ms did not result in differences in the reported results.
source: other time windows between 60–300 ms did not result in differences in the results reported here.
evidence: Control analysis testing robustness of results to time window choice.

claim: The number of visual cortical neurons activated by the stimulus increases with stimulus size.
source: Based on the dependency of the density of receptive fields on eccentricity in early visual structures (Van Essen et al., 1981; Erickson et al., 1989), we calculated that the number of visual cortical neurons activated by our stimulus should increase with stimulus size (Figure 1B).
evidence: Calculation based on known cortical magnification factors with citations, shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Psychophysical studies in humans have found that larger stimuli are associated with diminished perceptual performance.
source: It is therefore surprising that behavioral studies in humans have sometimes found that larger stimuli are associated with diminished perceptual performance (Tadin et al., 2003).
evidence: Citation to previous human psychophysical studies.

claim: Psychophysical suppression of behavioral performance in human subjects is strongly correlated with various markers of mental function, including schizophrenia, major depression, and I.Q.
source: Moreover, this psychophysical suppression of behavioral performance in human subjects is strongly correlated with various markers of mental function, including schizophrenia, major depression, and even I.Q (Tadin et al., 2006; Golomb et al., 2009; Melnick et al., 2013).
evidence: Citations to previous studies linking psychophysical suppression to mental function markers.

claim: Psychophysical suppression has previously been hypothesized to reflect the strength of neuronal surround suppression in individual cortical neurons.
source: These results have previously been hypothesized to reflect the strength of neuronal surround suppression in individual cortical neurons (Tadin et al., 2003; Churan et al., 2008)
evidence: Citation to previous hypotheses in the literature.

claim: If neuronal variability is independent across neurons, it can be eliminated by simply averaging the responses of many neurons.
source: If the variability is independent across neurons, it can be eliminated by simply averaging the responses of many neurons.
evidence: Statement based on established principles of population coding.

claim: When neuronal noise is independent, available information about the stimulus theoretically increases with neuronal population size.
source: In this case, the available information about the stimulus theoretically increases with neuronal population size (Zohary et al., 1994; Shadlen et al., 1996).
evidence: Theoretical principle with citations to foundational papers.

claim: Neuronal noise is usually correlated across nearby neurons.
source: However, in reality neuronal noise is usually correlated across nearby neurons
evidence: Statement of established finding in neuroscience.

claim: Noise correlations are thought to greatly influence the fidelity of a population code.
source: and such noise correlations are thought to greatly influence on the fidelity of a population code (Abbott and Dayan, 1999; Sompolinsky et al., 2001; Panzeri et al., 1999; Averbeck et al., 2006; Ecker et al., 2011).
evidence: Citations to theoretical and empirical studies on noise correlations.

claim: Current theories predict that stimulus information will increase or saturate as the size of the corresponding neuronal pool increases.
source: Still, current theories predict the stimulus information will increase or saturate as the size of the corresponding neuronal pool increases.
evidence: Summary of theoretical predictions from the literature.

claim: Area MT is thought to be causally involved in behavioral decisions for motion direction.
source: Area MT is thought to be causally involved in behavioral decisions for motion direction (Born and Bradley, 2005)
evidence: Citation to previous work establishing MT's role in motion perception.

claim: Area MT contains many neurons with responses that are modulated by stimulus size and contrast.
source: and it contains many neurons with responses that are modulated by stimulus size and contrast (Allman et al., 1985; Pack et al., 2005).
evidence: Citations to previous neurophysiological studies of MT.

claim: Neurons in early visual structures have small receptive fields.
source: Because neurons in early visual structures have small receptive fields, large stimuli recruit more neurons
evidence: Statement of established property of early visual cortex.

claim: Large stimuli recruit more neurons in early visual structures.
source: Because neurons in early visual structures have small receptive fields, large stimuli recruit more neurons, potentially leading to more effective coding of stimulus properties and correspondingly better behavioral performance.
evidence: Logical inference from the property of small receptive fields.

claim: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) that targets MT reduces the spatial suppression effect.
source: Indeed, transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) that targets MT reduces the spatial suppression effect (Tadin et al., 2011).
evidence: Citation to previous TMS study.

claim: The TMS protocols used to modulate spatial suppression are inhibitory.
source: However, the TMS protocols used to modulate spatial suppression are inhibitory
evidence: Statement about the nature of TMS protocols used in previous studies.

claim: TMS effects on spatial suppression could be interpreted as an effect on noise correlations.
source: and so one might just as easily interpret these results as an effect on noise correlations (Waterston and Pack, 2010).
evidence: Alternative interpretation with citation.

claim: Inhibitory connectivity plays a role both in generating surround suppression and in regulating noise correlations.
source: This interpretation is consistent with our results, assuming that inhibitory connectivity plays a role both in generating surround suppression and in regulating noise correlations (Tripp, 2012; Carandini and Heeger, 2012; Renart et al., 2010).
evidence: Inference from results with citations to theoretical and empirical work.

claim: People with schizophrenia show reduced spatial suppression.
source: Examples include people with schizophrenia (Tadin et al., 2006)
evidence: Citation to previous psychophysical study in clinical population.

claim: Older individuals show reduced spatial suppression.
source: and older individuals (Betts et al., 2005).
evidence: Citation to previous psychophysical study in aging population.

claim: Subjects with reduced spatial suppression may have deficits in GABAergic efficacy.
source: Although these subjects may have deficits in GABAergic efficacy (Tadin et al., 2006; Betts et al., 2005)
evidence: Citations to previous studies suggesting GABAergic mechanisms.

claim: The connection between GABAergic deficits and psychophysical spatial suppression could be through noise correlations.
source: our results suggest that the connection to psychophysical spatial suppression could also be through noise correlations, as these are necessary to produce any effect of neural surround suppression at the population level.
evidence: Inference from the modeling results.

claim: Surround suppression can increase the selectivity of the neuronal population to the smallest stimulus size while worsening selectivity at larger sizes.
source: Our simulation results suggest that surround suppression can increase the selectivity of the neuronal population to the smallest stimulus size in this task, while worsening the selectivity at larger sizes (Figure 5C; note performance for the 1° stimulus).
evidence: Results from model simulations shown in Figure 5C.

claim: One benefit of surround suppression might be in the tracking of small moving stimuli.
source: Therefore, one benefit of surround suppression might be in the tracking of small moving stimuli.
evidence: Inference from simulation results about functional benefits.

claim: Activity in clusters of surround-suppressed neurons has been found to be causally linked to the tracking of small targets in smooth pursuit.
source: Indeed, activity in clusters of surround-suppressed neurons has been found to be causally linked to the tracking of small targets in smooth pursuit (Born et al., 2000).
evidence: Citation to previous study on smooth pursuit.

claim: Neuronal variability in MT can account for the majority of motor variation in smooth pursuit.
source: The link between MT activity and smooth pursuit initiation has been further strengthened by the finding that neuronal variability in MT can account for the majority of motor variation in smooth pursuit (Osborne et al., 2005; Hohl et al., 2013).
evidence: Citations to previous studies on MT and smooth pursuit.

claim: Correlation structure in MT might limit the precision of pursuit initiation.
source: These observations have led to the suggestion that correlation structure in MT might limit the precision of pursuit initiation (Huang and Lisberger, 2009).
evidence: Citation to previous hypothesis about MT correlations and pursuit.

claim: The neurons that contribute most directly to pursuit initiation exhibit more advantageous correlation structure.
source: Our results suggest that such comparisons should take into account the center-surround properties of individual MT neurons, as the neurons that seem to contribute most directly to pursuit initiation (Born et al., 2000) exhibit more advantageous correlation structure (Figure 4A).
evidence: Inference from the correlation structure results shown in Figure 4A with citation.

claim: The pursuit initiation system might benefit from averaging the activity of many surround-suppressed MT neurons.
source: As a result, the pursuit initiation system might benefit from averaging the activity of many surround-supressed MT neurons.
evidence: Inference from the correlation structure findings.

claim: The weak correlation between single-neuron MT activity and pursuit can be explained by the advantageous correlation structure of surround-suppressed neurons.
source: This would explain both the weak correlation between single-neuron MT activity and pursuit and the relatively low choice probability of surround suppressed neurons in our perception task (Figure 2E).
evidence: Inference connecting multiple findings with reference to Figure 2E.

claim: Some models of smooth pursuit initiation involve both a motion opponency step and a normalization operation.
source: It is interesting in this regard that some models of smooth pursuit initiation (Hohl et al., 2013) involve both a motion opponency step and a normalization operation.
evidence: Citation to previous computational models of pursuit.

claim: Normalization in smooth pursuit models serves the function of computing a vector average of the MT population response.
source: Normalization in these models serves the function of computing a vector average of the MT population response
evidence: Description of computational function in cited models.

claim: Normalization affects the levels of noise correlations in a manner that accounts for trial-to-trial fluctuations in behavior.
source: and it also affects the levels of noise correlations in a manner that accounts for trial-to-trial fluctuations in behavior.
evidence: Description of model properties from cited work.

claim: Normalization may reshape the selectivity of the MT population response to favor the motion of small stimuli.
source: Our results suggest the additional function of reshaping the selectivity of the MT population response in such a way as to favor the motion of small stimuli, precisely as would be expected for a system that initiates orienting responses to moving objects in a natural environment (Lettvin et al., 1959).
evidence: Inference from results with citation to classic work on motion detection.

claim: Choice probability was significantly above 0.5 from approximately 100 to 200 ms after stimulus onset (p<0.01).
source: CP was significantly above 0.5 from approximately 100 to 200 ms after stimulus onset (p<0.01, permutation test).
evidence: Statistical analysis of time-resolved choice probability shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Choice probability decreased with receptive field eccentricity (r = -0.48, P = 0.05).
source: we found instead that choice probability decreased with receptive field eccentricity (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D; r = -0.48, P = 0.05).
evidence: Statistical analysis of choice probability versus eccentricity shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Monkeys likely based their decisions on neurons with receptive fields closer to the center of the stimulus.
source: This suggests that the monkeys likely based their decisions on neurons with receptive fields closer to the center of the stimulus, where motion information was present reliably on every trial.
evidence: Inference from the choice probability versus eccentricity relationship.

claim: Psychophysical suppression would be reduced if stimulus location was unpredictable from trial to trial.
source: It would therefore be interesting to study psychophysical suppression in a paradigm in which the stimulus location was unpredictable from trial to trial. We predict that psychophysical suppression would be reduced in this case, as would overall performance across sizes (Herrmann et al., 2010).
evidence: Prediction based on inference from results with citation.

claim: Subjects allocate resources according to the uncertainty associated with individual stimulus positions.
source: Previous work suggests that subjects allocate resources according to the uncertainty associated with individual stimulus positions (Pelli, 1985)
evidence: Citation to previous work on resource allocation.

claim: Surround suppression has been hypothesized to reduce correlations in natural inputs.
source: Surround suppression has often been hypothesized to reduce correlations in natural inputs (Snyder et al., 2014; Vinje and Gallant, 2002).
evidence: Citations to previous hypotheses about surround suppression.

claim: Neurons with strong surround suppression can exhibit larger or smaller noise correlations, depending on the strength of their signal correlations.
source: We find that neurons with strong surround suppression can exhibit larger or smaller noise correlations, depending on the strength of their signal correlations.
evidence: Summary of findings from the correlation structure analysis.

claim: The relationship between noise and signal correlations holds for all stimuli, even those that do not engage the receptive field surrounds strongly.
source: This relationship holds for all stimuli, even those that do not engage the receptive field surrounds strongly.
evidence: Observation from analysis across different stimulus conditions.

claim: The magnitude of noise correlations can be reduced by adaptation.
source: Previous studies have shown that the magnitude of rnoise is not fixed, but can be reduced by adaptation (Gutnisky and Dragoi, 2008)
evidence: Citation to previous study on adaptation effects.

claim: The magnitude of noise correlations can be reduced by learning.
source: learning (Gu et al., 2011)
evidence: Citation to previous study on learning effects.

claim: The magnitude of noise correlations can be reduced by attention.
source: and attention (Cohen and Maunsell, 2009; Mitchell et al., 2009).
evidence: Citations to previous studies on attention effects.

claim: Attention increases the effective contrast of the stimulus.
source: The latter is particularly relevant, because attention increases the effective contrast of the stimulus (Treue and Trujillo, 1999)
evidence: Citation to previous study on attention and contrast.

claim: Increased effective contrast also increases surround suppression.
source: which also increases surround suppression (Sundberg et al., 2009)
evidence: Citation to previous study on contrast and surround suppression.

claim: Increased effective contrast decreases noise correlations.
source: and decreases correlations (Kohn and Smith, 2005).
evidence: Citation to previous study on contrast and correlations.

claim: A single mechanism may account for the effects of attention and surround suppression on noise correlations.
source: Thus a single mechanism (Reynolds and Heeger, 2009) may account for the effects of attention and surround suppression on noise correlations, as implemented with divisive normalization (Tripp, 2012; Wiechert et al., 2010).
evidence: Inference with citations to theoretical frameworks.

claim: Attention can increase or decrease the strength of noise correlations, depending on the stimulus encoding of the neuron pairs.
source: Attention is also of interest because, like surround suppression, it can increase or decrease the strength of noise correlations, depending on the stimulus encoding of the neuron pairs (Ruff and Cohen, 2014).
evidence: Citation to previous study on differential effects of attention.

claim: Differential effects of attention on positive and negative noise correlations are particularly important in MT, where negative correlations are quite common.
source: These differential effects on positive and negative noise correlations are particularly important in MT, where negative correlations are quite common (Zohary et al., 1994; Huang and Lisberger, 2009).
evidence: Citations to previous studies documenting negative correlations in MT.

claim: Negative correlations in MT likely arise from motion-opponent mechanisms.
source: Negative correlations likely arise from motion-opponent mechanisms, in which the outputs of neurons with opposite direction tuning are subtracted.
evidence: Inference about the source of negative correlations based on known mechanisms.

claim: Motion-opponent effects are stronger in MT than in V1.
source: Such effects are stronger in MT than in V1 (Qian and Andersen, 1994)
evidence: Citation to previous comparative study.

claim: Motion-opponent mechanisms play an important role in decision-making models.
source: and they play an important role in decision-making models (Shadlen et al., 1996; Cohen and Newsome, 2009).
evidence: Citations to computational models incorporating motion opponency.

claim: The neuron density was set to 20 neurons/mm2 in the model.
source: The absolute number of neurons can then be obtained by multiplying the cortical footprint by a factor that indicates the number of neurons per millimeter. We set this factor to 20 neurons/mm2
evidence: Description of modeling parameter choice.

claim: A neuron density of 20 neurons/mm2 yielded a range of pool sizes comparable to those used in other studies.
source: which yielded a range of pool sizes comparable to those used in other studies (Shadlen et al., 1996) (Figure 1B).
evidence: Justification of parameter choice with citation and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: The range of pool sizes used is in the regime where population sensitivity is saturated.
source: The range ofpool sizes is in the regime where population sensitivity is saturated (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Results were qualitatively similar when neuron density was set to 40 neurons/mm2.
source: We verified that our results are robust with respect to this parameter re-running the simulations with a value of 40 neurons/mm2; the results were qualitatively similar to those reported here.
evidence: Control analysis testing robustness to parameter choice.

claim: All procedures conformed to the regulations established by the Canadian Council on Animal Care.
source: All procedures conformed to the regulations established by the Canadian Council on Animal Care and were approved by the Institutional Animal Care Committee of the Montreal Neurological Institute.
evidence: Statement of ethical compliance.

claim: All procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care Committee of the Montreal Neurological Institute.
source: All procedures conformed to the regulations established by the Canadian Council on Animal Care and were approved by the Institutional Animal Care Committee of the Montreal Neurological Institute.
evidence: Statement of ethical approval.

claim: Eye movements were monitored with an EyeLink1000 infrared eye tracking system with a sampling rate of 1000 Hz.
source: For both monkeys, eye movements were monitored with an EyeLink1000 infrared eye tracking system (SR Research) with a sampling rate of 1000 Hz.
evidence: Description of equipment used for eye tracking.

claim: Visual motion stimuli were displayed at 60 Hz at 1280 by 800 pixels resolution.
source: Visual motion stimuli were displayed at 60 Hz at 1280 by 800 pixels resolution
evidence: Description of stimulus display parameters.

claim: The viewing area subtended 60° × 40° at a viewing distance of 50 cm.
source: the viewing area subtended 60° × 40° at a viewing distance of 50 cm.
